mainTopic: Whether a son may be the court's agent to strike or curse his father, and why a son who strikes a condemned father is חייב while a stranger is פטור
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier argument: רבי שמעון holds that a person is פטור for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה. Then a new topic begins. The חכמים ask רב ששת whether a son may be the agent of בית דין to strike or curse his father. רב ששת says yes, because כבוד שמים comes first. A ברייתא with a קל וחומר seems to challenge him, but the גמרא reads it as the source for the general ban on hitting anyone. Next comes a ברייתא about a man going out to be executed: his son who hits or curses him is חייב, while a stranger is פטור. רב ששת sets this in a case where the father walks willingly. The גמרא then tries several reasons for why the stranger is פטור: the condemned man counts as a גברא קטילא, the blow was under a פרוטה, or פטור means only free from money. When these fail, it learns from the פסוק 'וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר' that only one who acts like 'your people' is protected, and later רב מרי reads it as one who endures among your people. The amud ends by asking why, then, the son is not פטור too, and the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי שמעון exempts labor not needed for its own sake
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges an earlier claim by pointing out that רבי שמעון holds a person is פטור for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But doesn't רבי שמעון say that for any forbidden labor that is not needed for its own purpose, a person is exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an argument from the previous part of the דף. It challenges an earlier explanation by quoting a known rule of רבי שמעון that does not seem to fit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא had linked a ruling to רבי שמעון. Now it objects that רבי שמעון famously exempts a person when he does a forbidden labor without wanting the labor's actual result. So it is hard to see how רבי שמעון could be the source of a ruling that makes someone liable in that kind of case.

keyTerms.meaning: A forbidden labor on שבת
Not needed for its own sake: the person does the act, but he does not want the result that makes it a forbidden labor
Exempt from punishment
But doesn't he say? (a formula used to raise a contradiction)

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not start a new topic. It continues an argument from just before this section, which is why it opens with 'ו' (and).

phrases.english: But doesn't Rabbi Shimon say:
any labor that is not needed for its own sake,
one is exempt for it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the argument from the previous part of the דף by challenging an attribution to רבי שמעון.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier claim that this ruling follows רבי שמעון
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי שמעון exempts a person for a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה, so a ruling that makes someone liable in such a case cannot easily be his.

steps.title: May a son be the court's agent to strike or curse his father?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask רב ששת whether a son may be appointed by בית דין to strike or curse his own father.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב ששת: may a son be made an agent to strike his father or curse him?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The חכמים ask רב ששת whether a son may carry out the court's punishment, either striking or cursing, when the person being punished is his own father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a son is strictly forbidden to strike or curse his father. But when בית דין punishes someone, a שליח does the striking or cursing on the court's behalf. The question is whether the son's special duty toward his father stops him from being that שליח.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked him (a real question that needs an answer)
What is the law?
An agent; here, the person who carries out the court's punishment
To strike him and to curse him

phrases.english: They asked Rav Sheshet:
A son, what is the law: may he be made an agent regarding his father,
phrases.notes: He means an agent of בית דין, the person who carries out the court's punishment.

phrases.english: to strike him and to curse him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, unrelated to the רבי שמעון discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a son may serve as the court's agent to strike or curse his father.

steps.title: The honor of Heaven comes first, so a son may be the agent
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that striking anyone is normally forbidden, yet the court's agent may do it because כבוד שמים comes first. The same is true for a son.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Is it permitted to strike someone else? No! Rather, the honor of Heaven comes first. Here too, the honor of Heaven comes first.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת rules that a son may be the court's agent. He makes his point with a comparison to striking any other person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah forbids striking or cursing any Jew, not only a parent. Even so, the court's agent may do it, because carrying out the court's punishment honors Heaven, and that outweighs a person's own honor. A father's honor is also only human honor, so כבוד שמים outweighs it as well.

keyTerms.meaning: And another person, who permitted him? (meaning: striking anyone is forbidden too)
The honor of Heaven
Takes precedence, comes first
Here too

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out a basic idea: the honor owed to a parent is real, but it cannot stand in the way of carrying out the court's command, because that serves Heaven.

phrases.english: He said to them:
And another person, who permitted him?
phrases.notes: He is asking a question that answers itself: striking or cursing any Jew is forbidden too, yet the court's agent may do it.

phrases.english: Rather, the honor of Heaven takes precedence.
Here too, the honor of Heaven takes precedence.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. Just as the agent may strike any other person because כבוד שמים comes first, a son may strike or curse his father as the court's agent.

steps.title: A ברייתא's קל וחומר about who must not strike
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a challenge to רב ששת from a ברייתא. The ברייתא argues: if even someone commanded to strike has a מצוה not to strike, then surely someone not commanded to strike has that מצוה too.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him from a ברייתא: If one who is commanded to strike him still has a מצוה not to strike him, isn't it logical that one who is not commanded to strike him also has a מצוה not to strike him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is bringing a ברייתא to challenge רב ששת. This step is only the setup: it quotes the ברייתא's קל וחומר, and the next lines will show how it disagrees with רב ששת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא compares two kinds of people. One is commanded to strike, yet he still has a מצוה not to strike beyond what he was commanded. The other is never commanded to strike at all. The phrase 'one who is not commanded to strike him' points to someone who is never commanded to strike, and the גמרא will use this against רב ששת's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection, usually from a ברייתא or משנה
And if... (the opening of a קל וחומר)
Is it not logical? (the conclusion of a קל וחומר)
A מצוה not to strike him

steps.confusionAlert: The challenge is not finished here. These lines only quote the ברייתא, and the גמרא explains how it contradicts רב ששת right after this.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
And if one who is commanded to strike him,
has a מצוה not to strike him,
phrases.notes: He means not to strike beyond what he was commanded.

phrases.english: then one who is not commanded to strike him,
is it not logical that there is a מצוה not to strike him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a challenge to רב ששת's answer in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that a son may serve as the court's agent to strike his father
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא speaks of 'one who is not commanded to strike him', which suggests someone who is never commanded to strike. The גמרא will argue that this does not fit רב ששת's view that a son may strike his father as the court's agent.

steps.title: Reading the ברייתא as forbidding a son even when striking is a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that both clauses of the ברייתא deal with a מצוה situation. The 'commanded' clause means another person and the 'not commanded' clause means the son. That reading would contradict רב ששת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it that both parts of the ברייתא are talking about a case where striking is a מצוה? One part is about the son, and the other part is about another person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes the challenge to רב ששת that started in the last step. It explains how the ברייתא could be read to forbid a son from striking his father, even as the court's agent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spoke of 'one commanded to strike' and 'one not commanded to strike.' The גמרא suggests both are court agents in a מצוה situation. Under that reading, the son counts as 'not commanded' to hit his own father, so he may not do it, which goes against רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it that...? (the גמרא proposes a reading of a source)
Both this and that (both clauses)
In a situation where striking is a מצוה
Another person (not the son)

phrases.english: Is it not that both this and that
are in a situation where striking is a מצוה?
This one is about his son,
phrases.notes: This is the clause about someone 'not commanded' to strike.

phrases.english: and that one is about another person.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי לָאו אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בִּמְקוֹם מִצְוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge begun in step 4 by explaining how the ברייתא contradicts רב ששת.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that a son may strike his father as the court's agent
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If both clauses deal with a מצוה situation, the only difference left is son versus stranger. That would mean a son may not strike his father even when the court commands it.

steps.title: The ברייתא contrasts מצוה and non-מצוה situations, not son and stranger
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects that reading. In both clauses, son and stranger are treated the same. The difference is whether striking is a מצוה or not.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. In both parts there is no difference between the son and another person. It is not difficult: one part is about a situation where striking is a מצוה, and the other is about a situation where it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב ששת by giving the ברייתא a different meaning. The two clauses are about two different situations, not two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the ברייתא is not about a son at all, it says nothing against רב ששת. The contrast is between a מצוה situation, like a court agent giving lashes, and a non-מצוה situation, like ordinary hitting. A son and a stranger follow the same rule in each case.

keyTerms.meaning: There is no difference
And it is not difficult (this is how the contradiction is resolved)
Here... there (each clause refers to a different case)
In a situation where striking is not a מצוה

phrases.english: No, in both this and that

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא בְּנוֹ וְלָא שְׁנָא אַחֵר.
phrases.english: it makes no difference whether it is his son or another person.
And it is not difficult:
here, it is in a situation where striking is a מצוה,
there, it is in a situation where striking is not a מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5 by rereading the two clauses of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the source: the clauses differ by situation, not by person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clauses contrast a son with a stranger, both acting as court agents.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clauses contrast a מצוה situation with a non-מצוה situation, and a son is the same as anyone else.

steps.title: Rereading the ברייתא as a קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out the ברייתא under the new reading. Even a court agent, who must strike, has a מצוה not to add extra blows. So surely an ordinary person, who has no מצוה to strike, must not strike at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what the ברייתא teaches: In a situation where striking is a מצוה, where one is commanded to strike him, there is still a מצוה not to strike him beyond what is required. So in a situation where striking is not a מצוה, where one is not commanded to strike him, isn't it logical that there is a מצוה not to strike him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how the ברייתא reads word by word under its new explanation. This finishes the defense of רב ששת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is a קל וחומר: if a court agent is warned not to add even one extra lash, an ordinary person is surely warned not to hit at all. This is the source for the general ban on striking another person. Nothing here forbids a son from acting as the court's agent.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what it teaches (rereading a source's wording)
If... then is it not logical? (the wording of a קַל וָחוֹמֶר)
To strike him

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא is not about sons. It is a קל וחומר from the court agent's extra-lash warning to the general ban on hitting anyone. So רב ששת still stands.

phrases.english: And this is what it teaches:
And just as in a situation where striking is a מצוה,
where it is a מצוה to strike him,
there is a מצוה not to strike him;
phrases.notes: He means not one lash more than the court set, as it says in דברים 25:3.

phrases.english: then in a situation where striking is not a מצוה,
where it is not a מצוה to strike him,
is it not logical that there is a מצוה not to strike him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the full wording of the ברייתא according to the answer given in step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source's wording as a קל וחומר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא limits what a son may do as the court's agent.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא derives the general ban on striking from the court agent's warning not to add lashes.

steps.title: A new challenge: a son who strikes his father on the way to execution
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a son who strikes or curses his father on the way to execution is חייב, while a stranger is פטור. רב חסדא explains this is when the father refuses to go and force is needed. That suggests a son may not hit his father even when hitting is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If a man is going out to be executed, and his son came and struck him or cursed him, the son is liable. If another person came and struck him or cursed him, he is exempt. We discussed this: why is the son different from another person? And רב חסדא said: this is a case where they are urging him to go out and he refuses to go.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to challenge רב ששת. It sets up the point that even when the court allows force, a son is still liable for hitting his father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא puts the ברייתא in a case where the condemned man refuses to walk, so pushing or hitting him is permitted. Even so, the son is חייב. That looks like a son may not strike his father even when striking is permitted, which seems to go against רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (a new source is brought)
One who is going out to be executed
Liable / exempt
And we discussed it (refers to an earlier discussion of this ברייתא)
Urging, pressing someone who refuses

steps.confusionAlert: רב חסדא's line is not the final answer to the challenge. It explains the ברייתא, and that explanation is what creates the problem for רב ששת.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who is going out to be executed,
and his son came and struck him or cursed him, he is liable;
if another person came and struck him or cursed him, he is exempt.
And we discussed it:

phrases.aramaic: מַאי שְׁנָא בְּנוֹ וּמַאי שְׁנָא אַחֵר?
phrases.english: Why is the son different, and why is another person different?
And רב חסדא said:
It is when they urge him to go out and he does not go out.
phrases.notes: So force is needed to move him. The court allows hitting here, yet the son is still liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first challenge was answered, the גמרא brings a new ברייתא against רב ששת.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that a son may strike his father when the court allows it
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In רב חסדא's case, force against the condemned man is permitted, yet the son is still חייב. So a son seems to be forbidden to strike his father even in a permitted, court-backed situation.

steps.title: רב ששת: the father is walking willingly
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the ברייתא is about a father who is not refusing to go out to his execution.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת explains the ברייתא as talking about a case where they do not need to push the father to go out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 8 by giving the ברייתא a different setting. In this setting the father walks out on his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא read the ברייתא as a case where force was needed, so hitting would be allowed. רב ששת says no: nobody needs to hit the father here. That means the son is hitting when there is no permission to hit, so his liability says nothing against רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: He sets it up as / explains it as talking about
Refusing, resisting (or: pressing someone who resists)
To go out (to the place of execution)

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet sets it up
in a case where they are not urging him to go out.
phrases.notes: The father is walking to his execution on his own, so nobody needs to force him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 8 by placing the ברייתא in a different case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא is about a father who refuses to go, so hitting him is allowed, and still the son is חייב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a father who goes willingly, so there is no permission to hit him at all.

steps.title: Then a stranger should be liable too
steps.stepSummary: If nobody is allowed to hit the father here, why is a stranger פטור?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, another person should also be liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new setting from step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there is no permission to hit, then hitting is just plain forbidden hitting. Plain forbidden hitting is wrong for anyone, so the ברייתא's ruling that a stranger is פטור seems hard to understand.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Another person, a stranger (not the son)

phrases.english: If so, another person too?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the setting proposed in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's setting of the ברייתא (a father walking willingly)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without any permission to hit, a stranger who hits should also be חייב, yet the ברייתא says he is פטור.

steps.title: A condemned man counts as a dead man
steps.stepSummary: A stranger is פטור because a person sentenced to death is treated as already dead.
steps.simpleTranslation: A stranger is פטור because the condemned man is considered a dead man.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the stranger is פטור even in רב ששת's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stranger's ruling has nothing to do with permission to hit. Since the man is about to be executed, he is treated as a 'killed man', so a stranger does not get punished for hitting him. The son is different because the honor he owes his father stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: A 'killed man', someone treated as already dead

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean hitting him is allowed. It means a stranger is not punished for it.

phrases.english: As for another person, this is a killed man.
phrases.notes: Since he's about to be executed, the condemned man is treated as if he's already dead.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New reason for the stranger's ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A stranger should be חייב for hitting without permission.
steps.terutzMaskana: A stranger is פטור because the condemned man counts as a גברא קטילא.

steps.title: רב ששת's own case of shaming a sleeping man
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת himself rules that someone who shames a sleeping man who then dies is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רב ששת said: if someone shamed a sleeping man and the man died, the shamer is חייב!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 11 from another ruling of רב ששת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sleeping man who dies without waking never felt the shame, and still the shamer must pay. So a condemned man, even if he is 'like dead', should still be owed payment for being shamed. That makes it hard to say the stranger is fully פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? (opens a challenge)
He shamed him (בושת, payment for embarrassment)
Sleeping, and then he died

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Sheshet say:
if he shamed him while he was sleeping, and he died, he is liable?
phrases.notes: The man never woke up to feel the shame, yet the payment still goes to his heirs.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: בִּיְּישׁוֹ יָשֵׁן וָמֵת – חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the גברא קטילא reasoning of step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a stranger is פטור because the condemned man is a גברא קטילא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב ששת makes a shamer pay even when the victim never felt it and died. So a 'dead-like' condemned man should also be owed payment.

steps.title: The blow was worth less than a פרוטה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is about a blow too small to cause damage worth a פרוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where he hit him with a blow that does not have a פרוטה's worth of damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing the ברייתא to a very small blow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Money is only owed for damage worth at least a פרוטה. If the blow was smaller than that, there is nothing to pay. So the stranger is פטור, and this does not clash with רב ששת's shaming ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?
A blow, a strike
Worth a פרוטה, the smallest amount of money that counts

phrases.english: What are we dealing with here?
In a case where he hit him with a blow
that does not have a perutah's worth in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The stranger should owe payment, like the man who shamed a sleeping person.
steps.terutzMaskana: The blow was under a פרוטה, so there is no payment at all.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: even a tiny blow gets lashes
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that a blow worth less than a פרוטה is punished with מלקות.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי אמי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: one who hits another with a blow worth less than a פרוטה gets lashes!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 13 with a ruling of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the blow is under a פרוטה, there is no money to pay, so the hitter gets מלקות instead. If so, how can the ברייתא call the stranger פטור?

keyTerms.meaning: He gets lashes (מלקות)

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Ami say that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: הִכָּהוּ הַכָּאָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה
phrases.english: if he hit him with a blow that does not have a perutah's worth in it
he gets lashes?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the 'less than a פרוטה' setting of step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that the stranger is פטור in a case of a blow under a פרוטה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A blow under a פרוטה brings מלקות, so the stranger should not be called פטור.

steps.title: Exempt only from paying money
steps.stepSummary: 'פטור' in the ברייתא means free from paying money, not free from all punishment.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does the 'פטור' that it says mean? פטור from money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the word 'פטור' more narrowly. The next step rejects this answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא never said the stranger has no punishment at all. It only said he pays no money. He can still get מלקות, just like רבי יוחנן says, so everything fits together.

keyTerms.meaning: Free from paying money

steps.whatToRemember: This 'free from money only' answer does not last. Step 16 rejects it, and step 17 gives a new reason why the stranger is פטור.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer tries to keep the 'less than a פרוטה' setting of the ברייתא alive. The very next step rejects it.

phrases.english: What is the 'exempt' that it says?
Exempt from money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 14 by reading the ברייתא's word 'פטור' narrowly.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the meaning of a word
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'פטור' means the stranger has no punishment at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'פטור' means free from paying money only. He still gets מלקות.

steps.title: The son's 'liable' cannot mean money, so the stranger's 'exempt' cannot either
steps.stepSummary: If 'פטור' for the stranger means only free from money, then 'חייב' for the son would mean he must pay money. That cannot be right. 'חייב' for the son must mean he gets his real punishment, so 'פטור' for the stranger must also mean free from his real punishment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Would that mean the son is liable to pay money? No. Rather, the son is liable to the punishment that fits him. So here too, the stranger is exempt from the punishment that fits him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the answer from step 15. It points out that the same ברייתא uses 'חייב' for the son, and that word cannot be about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא sets the son and the stranger side by side, so 'חייב' and 'פטור' have to be talking about the same thing. The son's 'חייב' clearly means his real punishment, not money. So the stranger's 'פטור' must mean he gets no punishment at all, and that brings back the problem raised by רבי יוחנן in step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: Implying / you could conclude from this
According to his proper punishment
With money (paying damages)
Here too

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not the גמרא's own final answer. It is an attack on step 15, which reopens the question 'why is the stranger פטור?'. Step 17 gives a new answer.

phrases.english: Would that imply that his son is liable to pay money?
Rather, he is liable to his proper punishment.
Here too, the stranger is exempt from his proper punishment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 15 by comparing it to the other half of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 15's claim that 'פטור' means only free from paying money
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two halves of the ברייתא must use 'liable' and 'exempt' in the same way. The son's 'liable' is not about money, so the stranger's 'exempt' is not about money either.

steps.title: A new reason: the פסוק protects only someone acting like 'your people'
steps.stepSummary: The stranger is פטור because the פסוק 'וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר' teaches that the ban on cursing protects only a person who behaves the way 'your people' should behave. A man condemned to death for his crime is not acting that way.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is the reason the stranger is exempt: the פסוק says, 'And a ruler among your people you shall not curse.' This means only one who does the deeds of your people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a brand-new reason why the stranger is פטור. It drops the earlier answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'בְעַמְּךָ', 'among your people', limit who is protected. The ban covers only someone who acts like a proper member of the Jewish people. A person sentenced to death for his sin falls outside that protection, so a stranger who curses him is פטור even from מלקות.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the reason
And a ruler among your people you shall not curse
One who does the deeds of your people (acts like a proper Jew)
The פסוק

steps.whyThisMatters: This idea, that the protection depends on how the person behaves, is the key to the rest of the סוגיא.

phrases.english: Rather, this is the reason the stranger is exempt:
Because the verse says:
"And a ruler among your people you shall not curse"
Meaning, only one who does the deeds of your people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 16 brings back the problem, this step gives a completely new reason why the stranger is פטור.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the stranger is פטור because a condemned man counts as dead, or because the blow was too small.
steps.terutzMaskana: The stranger is פטור because the protection covers only someone who acts like 'your people', and a condemned sinner does not.

steps.title: The פסוק only talks about cursing, so what about hitting?
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is about cursing. Where do we learn that the same rule applies to hitting?
steps.simpleTranslation: That works for cursing. But for hitting, where do we learn it from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question on step 17. The פסוק speaks only about cursing, but the ברייתא is also about hitting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new reason comes from a פסוק that bans cursing. The ברייתא makes the stranger פטור for hitting too, so the גמרא needs a source that carries the rule over to hitting.

keyTerms.meaning: That works well for
Cursing
Hitting
From where do we know?

phrases.english: That works well for cursing;
from where do we know it for hitting?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out that the source in step 17 covers only cursing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק mentions only cursing, so on its own it cannot explain why the stranger is פטור for hitting.

steps.title: Hitting is compared to cursing
steps.stepSummary: We compare hitting to cursing, so the same rule applies to both.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because we compare hitting to cursing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that hitting and cursing are treated the same, so whatever is true for cursing is also true for hitting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה links hitting a parent with cursing a parent, so the two are compared to each other. Because of that link, the rule that only someone acting like 'your people' is protected applies to hitting too.

keyTerms.meaning: We compare (one law to another, so they share the same rules)

phrases.english: Because we compare hitting to cursing.
phrases.notes: In the תורה, hitting a father and cursing a father show up close together, so the two are linked (שמות 21:15, 21:17).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18 by linking hitting to cursing.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule from the פסוק might apply only to cursing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Hitting is compared to cursing, so the same rule applies to both.

steps.title: Then the son should be פטור too
steps.stepSummary: If a condemned man is not protected because he is not acting like 'your people', then his own son should also be פטור. But the ברייתא says the son is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, his son too should be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reason from step 17. It seems to free the son as well, which goes against the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason in step 17 is about the condemned man himself: he is not acting like 'your people'. That fact does not change depending on who hits him. So the reason seems to free the son too, but the ברייתא says the son is חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
His son

phrases.english: If so, his son too should be exempt?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the reason from step 17 to raise a problem with the son's half of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason from step 17 ('one who does the deeds of your people')
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the father loses his protection because of how he acted, the son should also be פטור. Yet the ברייתא says the son is חייב.

steps.title: The condemned man did תשובה
steps.stepSummary: Following רב פינחס, the ברייתא is talking about a case where the condemned man did תשובה. So he again counts as acting like 'your people', and his son is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב פינחס said: when he did תשובה. Here too, it is talking about when he did תשובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers using an idea from רב פינחס: the condemned man did תשובה, so he is protected again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doing תשובה puts the man back into the group of 'one who does the deeds of your people', even though he will still be put to death. That is why his son is חייב for hitting or cursing him.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא whose idea is used here
When he did תשובה (repented)
So too / the same here

steps.whatToRemember: The stranger is פטור because a condemned sinner is not 'one who does the deeds of your people'. Hitting is learned from cursing through the comparison. The son's case in the ברייתא is about a father who did תשובה.
steps.confusionAlert: The answer explains why the son is חייב. It does not yet explain why the stranger would still be פטור if the father did תשובה. Step 22 raises exactly this problem, and step 23 answers it.

phrases.english: As רב פינחס said:
It is talking about when he did תשובה.
Here too, it is when he did תשובה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 by explaining what kind of case the son's half of the ברייתא is about.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A condemned man never counts as acting like 'your people', so his son should be פטור.
steps.terutzMaskana: Once he did תשובה, he counts as acting like 'your people' again, so his son is חייב.

steps.title: If he did תשובה, a stranger should be חייב too
steps.stepSummary: If the condemned man did תשובה and counts again as 'acting like your people,' then a stranger who hits or curses him should also be חייב. But the ברייתא says the stranger is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then another person should also be liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב פינחס's answer. If תשובה puts the condemned man back under the protection of 'your people,' that should apply to everyone, not just his son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 used תשובה to explain why the son is חייב. But תשובה changes the condemned man's own status, and that status should matter to everyone. So the answer now clashes with the first half of the ברייתא, which says a stranger is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if what you just said is true)
Another person, a stranger (not the son)
Also, too

phrases.english: If so, another person too?
phrases.notes: He means: if the condemned man did תשובה, a stranger who hits or curses him should also be חייב.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תירוץ of רב פינחס in step 21 by showing it clashes with the stranger's פטור in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פינחס's explanation that the ברייתא is talking about a condemned man who did תשובה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: תשובה restores his status as 'acting like your people.' That status protects him from everyone, so the stranger should be חייב as well, which contradicts the ברייתא.

steps.title: רב מרי: the protection is only for someone who will go on living among the people
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי reads 'בְּעַמְּךָ' as 'one who is enduring among your people.' A condemned man is about to be killed, so even if he did תשובה, a stranger is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי said: 'Among your people' means one who endures (lives on) among your people.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי gives a new way to read the פסוק so that the stranger stays פטור even when the condemned man did תשובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, 'בְּעַמְּךָ' was read as 'acting like your people,' and תשובה could fix that. Now רב מרי reads it as 'staying alive among your people.' תשובה does not change the fact that he is about to be executed, so the stranger remains פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives this answer
Among your people (from the פסוק 'וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר')
Enduring, someone who stays alive and continues to exist

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the same reading as before. Earlier 'בְּעַמְּךָ' meant 'behaving like your people.' רב מרי's reading is about 'remaining alive among your people,' which תשובה cannot change.

phrases.english: Rav Mari said:
"Among your people": one who endures among your people.
phrases.notes: שמות 22:27. A man on his way to be executed won't be staying among the people, so this protection doesn't cover him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי: בְּעַמְּךָ – בִּמְקוּיָּם שֶׁבְּעַמְּךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 22 by giving the word 'בְּעַמְּךָ' a new meaning.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought 'בְּעַמְּךָ' meant 'acting like your people,' so תשובה would make the stranger חייב too.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'בְּעַמְּךָ' means 'enduring among your people.' A man about to be executed is not enduring, so a stranger is פטור even after his תשובה.

steps.title: Then the son should be פטור too
steps.stepSummary: If a condemned man is not protected because he will not endure among the people, his son should also be פטור. But the ברייתא says the son is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then his son should also be exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב מרי's reading. Being about to die has nothing to do with who does the hitting, so the son should be פטור like everyone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב מרי's reading solved the problem of the stranger but brings back the problem of the son from step 20. The condemned man is no more 'enduring' when his son hits him than when a stranger does. The גמרא now needs a reason why the son is different.

keyTerms.meaning: His son

phrases.english: If so, his son too?
phrases.notes: He means the son should also be פטור, yet the ברייתא says the son is חייב.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב מרי's answer in step 23 by bringing back the son question from step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מרי's reading of 'בְּעַמְּךָ' as 'enduring among your people.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being about to die is a fact about the condemned man himself. It applies equally to his son, so the son should be פטור, which contradicts the ברייתא.
